steps.label: The method and the conditions
lines: Air is passed over white-hot coke, that

The temperature is kept at about 1273 K.

The nitrogen of the air does not react.

steps.why: Air, not pure oxygen, is what makes this gas what it is. Air contains about four parts of nitrogen for every one part of oxygen, and since the nitrogen does not react it stays in the product and dilutes it.
common_mistakes: Writing that steam is passed over the coke. Steam gives water gas; air is what gives producer gas.
Writing that the nitrogen reacts with the carbon. Nitrogen passes through unchanged at this temperature.
steps.memory_tip: Air over hot coke: the oxygen becomes carbon monoxide and the nitrogen passes through with it.
steps.margin_note: Name air and white-hot coke, and say clearly that the nitrogen does not react.

steps.label: The balanced equation
lines: Atoms: 2 C, 2 O and 8 N on each side.
The 4N₂ is written on both sides because
air contains about four parts of
nitrogen to one part of oxygen, and the
The mixture of CO and N₂ collected is
steps.why: Two carbon atoms are needed for one oxygen molecule, because one oxygen atom combines with each carbon atom to give carbon monoxide. The nitrogen is written on both sides to show the composition of the air and of the gas produced.
common_mistakes: Writing CO₂ as the product. Only one oxygen atom combines with each carbon atom here, so the product is carbon monoxide.
Leaving the nitrogen out of the equation. Writing it on both sides is what shows why producer gas contains so much nitrogen.
steps.memory_tip: Two carbons for one oxygen molecule, and the four nitrogen molecules of the air pass through unchanged, so they appear on both sides.
steps.margin_note: Count the atoms on both sides. The nitrogen is unchanged, so the same 4N₂ appears left and right.

insider_note: The whole difference from water gas is one word: air instead of steam. Writing the nitrogen on both sides of the equation is what explains the composition of producer gas and why it burns poorly.
